item.title: Collaborative work groups on exposition problems
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Fear of being scooped leads to unpolished preprints intended to claim priority. Could such undesirable flag-planting behavior also arise for expository work on key results? Starting from this premise, this post proposes that collaborative working groups offer a healthier way forward.
item.content:encoded:
Alexander Van Werde, Postdoctoral Researcher at Mathematics Münster, Germany

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

A significant worry in our community is a potential widening gap between human understanding and formal problem solutions. This issue has been increasingly apparent due to AI systems’ ability to generate long formally verified proofs. A common sentiment is that it would help if we assigned more credit to exposition.

A related issue is the pressure that authors experience to put an unpolished preprint online to avoid being scooped. Sometimes, this unpolished state may only be temporary. However, the expertise needed to polish the writeup is not always present for AI-generated results. The expertise required for a first proof was reduced by AI systems, but it is likely still needed for digestion and exposition.

Could the rush that leads to unpolished preprints arise for exposition too? If an author gets recognized for an acceptable writeup, then others may get less credit for better exposition. For well-known problems, it is plausible that multiple people are working independently. This makes accidental scooping more likely, so authors might be incentivized to rush.

One approach is for authors to announce that they are working on it. However, this encourages the exact flag-planting behavior that initial unpolished preprints are associated with. Moreover, others may also want to digest the ideas, and collaboration could be beneficial!

I propose that it may be better to announce collaborative work groups:

  1. Someone in the field, who may not be the original author, forms a group intended to work on the exposition and digestion of a preprint. This group announces its existence. Further, the group states what additional expertise it would benefit from.
  2. The group creates a blog or Git repository where it openly reports on partial progress. For instance, an initial report could discuss the previous literature, addressing a common problem in AI-generated manuscripts. Subsequent reports could release expositions on parts of the technical content, as the digestion proceeds.

    Such reports would be valuable to the community. The ideas used to resolve a central problem may also be relevant elsewhere, so having some quick updates would be useful. Further, this would make it clear that the group is not merely a flag-planting operation.

The end goal could be to produce a human-written manuscript with good exposition that can be submitted at classical venues. This would allow the hard work of exposition to be acknowledged within the incentive structures that currently exist.

The reasons why such groups could be particularly suitable for expository work are as follows:

  1. A single author asserting ownership feels silly when the solution was generated by an autonomous AI system. The solution then properly belongs to the community. An open collaborative approach would hence be more natural, while still rewarding the people that worked on the exposition with demonstrable research output.
  2. The engagement of a group of people would help to disseminate the ideas. This group would naturally be trained to pursue and appreciate follow-up activities, such as searching for generalizations or applications of the tools in different problems.
  3. While a proof can in principle be generated and formally verified in an arbitrarily short time span, human digestion has natural limits. Hence, the latter activity particularly requires a slower process. This would be aided by the protection from accidental scooping that follows from the announcement of the group’s existence.

Such groups do not need to be huge. Having too many collaborators incurs communication difficulties and can lead to “design by committee” where the exposition lacks a unified vision. However, the idea is that the term “collaborative work group” would signal an open attitude, where collaborators are welcome subject to reasonable constraints. Initial arXiv announcements of unpolished preprints often feel like an author marking their territory, the exact opposite signal.

I am curious what others think. It appears that a central repository with such work group announcements could be useful. There could however also be downsides. For example, the act of engaging with improperly written preprints might appear to legitimize their production.

This is a condensed version of a post on the author’s blog.

item.title: A new system of accreditation
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts

item.content:encoded:
Andrew Ng, PhD student at the University of Bonn

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

It has become clear in recent years, and especially after the advent of LLMs, that the current publication system of journals is untenable and inequitable. I think this is an excellent opportunity to reform the system, so let me outline a suggestion.

I propose the following: the main way that a mathematician obtains “credit” for new results should be by writing publications which are at the level of doctoral theses and defending them in front of the mathematical community. The community can then give this publicly available reviews. Hiring committees then look at someone’s list of such publications, taking into account the community’s comments to judge quality if they so desire, and make hiring decisions based on that.

Concretely, how this would work is the following. Every year, everybody who has defended a PhD thesis has the right to ask for a defence of one of their preprints. (PhD theses are defended the same way as before.)

These are not submitted to any journals; we abolish journals by agreeing that nothing which is received from the 1st of January 2029 will be refereed or quick opinioned or given any of the unpaid and unacknowledged labour that journals need to function. In place of journals, some sort of international organisation, such as the IMU, receives requests from mathematicians to defend a preprint, which is uploaded to said organisation’s website and/or the arXiv. For simplicity’s sake let’s pretend that the IMU does this so I don’t have to write international organisation, but I want to emphasise that it need not be the IMU or any existing organisation: it could be a new thing entirely. The IMU then appoints someone to examine the publication, akin to how examiners examine doctoral theses. Theses should be tagged with keywords/ MSC codes etc, and all mathematicians who have defended a thesis or publication in related areas have the right to rate this by writing comments on a system hosted by the IMU’s server. These are publicly available and must be tied to the reviewing mathematician somehow. For instance, one might have to use ORCID to access this system, but the ORCID would not be publicly available (probably only to the examiner, if at all). The criteria used could be elegance of the argument, novelty of the techniques, and depth, as measured by establishing connections to other problems which are not obviously related or connections to other areas of mathematics.1

After a period of at least 3 months (also subject to debate, but some time so that there is enough time for others to read the publication and for the author incorporate comments, corrections etc.), a defence of the preprint should take place, broadcast online so that other people may take part. The purpose of this is for the author to convince the community of the correctness and interest of the results in the preprint, and to explain the proof/methods to all those who are interested. I cannot stress the importance of the latter enough: it is imperative that we cure ourselves of Hardy’s disease2. All present should additionally rate the defence on quality of exposition. At the end of the defence, the examiner should compile the opinions of the mathematicians who have rated the preprint, decide whether the defence was successful, and write a longer report. If successful, the preprint is published along with the examiner’s report and all the opinions of others who have rated them. The quality of a publication is judged by the examiner’s report and the collective opinion of the mathematicians who have rated it, but there are no more or less prestigious “places” to defend since all defences are centrally administered. This sort of publication is what is considered in the “proving results” part of hiring/promotion decisions.

Why do this, and how do other existing practices change/adapt?

This may sound like a lot of work. That’s because it is. However, I believe that in the age of generative LLMs a publication should merit this amount of work in order to be deserving of publication. As we all know by now, just having a proof of some theorem is not indicative of anything. It should form part of some larger body of work that points to new directions in research, and that is what, allegedly, a doctoral thesis is meant to be.

Since this is a lot of work for the examiner in particular, I believe that in career-related decisions, committees should weight examining a publication as highly as defending one. Examiners should be given credit for their work regardless of acceptance. Since the examiner is supposed to understand the publication well, responsibility for explanation and exposition of the results in the publication should fall on both the author and the examiner.

I think this proposal has a reasonable claim to stopping the arms race in publishing papers. I have heard senior people lament that students are now pressured to publish papers earlier and earlier, and that has the effect that often students don’t think about things as deeply as they used to. The proposed system incentivises everybody, not just PhD students, to think deeply about whatever mathematics they are engaged in. To prevent people from just shoving random results together and calling that a preprint, I suggest that we give the examiners the right to say that the results of a preprint are incoherent and there is no unifying theme. I would also say that preprints can be defended jointly if most of the results were obtained in collaboration, but the preprint should count towards the quota of all the authors.

I believe that a defence where one can grill the speaker is much better for communicating understanding/expositional purposes. I agree with Frank Calegari here that “the median mathematics seminar could (perhaps harshly) be described as a waste of time for both the participants and the speaker”. In talks where I am actually interested in the speaker’s results, I have found the introductory spiel to be uninspiring, and to take up too much time so that the new results are only very cursorily alluded to. I cannot press the speaker on the details of their methods, because this could be considered heckling, derail the conference schedule, and disturb their flow. Consequently, I get nothing out of the talk and have to resort to pestering the speaker afterwards. I think if we really wanted to get anything more than a superficial acquaintance with the speaker’s work out of a talk, that talk has to resemble a doctoral defence more than it does a conference talk in the current model.

What of the arXiv? I think this is a great endeavour and we should work to preserve it. I think people should continue uploading preprints to the arXiv, and that the authors of a preprint have the right to use the results in it in a defence and call those “their results” for the next two years3 after uploading. This is so that people can stake claims to results and not get scooped while they work on building their narrative. After the two year period, the results should be considered as folklore4: they can be used by anyone in a defence. The purpose of having an expiry date at all is this: some people choose not to fully explain or clean up their arguments, sometimes never publishing them. This results in an undesirable situation: obviously someone should do this work so that it can be verified, digested, and incorporated into the community’s repertoire, but there is currently no incentive to do this, since it would be, generally speaking, unacknowledged labour. Having an expiry date rewards someone who is willing to put in the effort to understand the mathematics in an orphaned preprint and integrate it into the community. This also deals with the issue of AI company produced preprints. Let’s take the construction of a complex structure on S6S^6 as an example. Engel took the initial 100 page preprint and turned it into a much more readable 20 page preprint (although I tried to read it, it is still beyond me since I don’t have the background in complex geometry, but I am told it is much better). In my proposed system, the result is his to claim, and I think this is fair.

While we are on the topic of reforming the system, I would also like to propose that the IMU have a dedicated branch towards public outreach and exposition, and substantial contributions towards this goal should be weighted the same as contributions such as defending or examining publications. Converting mathematics into something that the general public can appreciate is very hard work which deserves to be recognised. The public has funded our research and they deserve to get something out of it as well. If we do not want to rely on the blood money of the finance and tech companies and be beholden to their whims, we must convince the public that what we do is of value to them5. I admit that I do not know how best to do this, but there are many people who have experience with successfully engaging with the public, and that expertise should be tapped.

I have dreamt up this system based on the assumption that it is depth of understanding that we want to preserve and encourage. I would like to address the concern that this is somehow unfair to the people who prefer problem solving, and I will say what I mean using combinatorics as an example. I think that it is fine to enjoy problem solving. I do. But I think that when doing research, especially in this day and age, just solving the problem isn’t enough. One should find better and/or alternative ways of solving the problem6, and try to hit on methods/techniques/heuristics which apply more generally. For instance, Turan’s theorem has a number of different proofs, many of which generalise to other problems or hint at more general theory which can be explored. If, in a hypothetical universe which had adopted this system, somebody had discovered what we call Turan’s theorem, then what they could do next is solve more Turan like problems and publish a treatise on forbidden subgraphs. Similarly, Erdos’ introduction of the probabilistic method to bound Ramsey numbers is an ingenious and extremely elegant argument, and one which is taught to many undergraduates for good reason: it generalises. If someone had discovered the probabilistic method, they could then prove some number of other results that were previously inaccessible and then write a publication on this method and how great and good it is. I have been taught, and have taught others, that solving problems helps you solve more problems. Research papers should show this in action.

LLMs

I have thus far been a bit coy about the exact status of LLMs in mathematics in this proposed universe. Only time will tell, but from my perspective the current unregulated system poses an existential risk comparable to that of nuclear weapons, if not worse. In my opinion, private companies absolutely should not be allowed to train any sort of large language model or AI. I agree with others who believe that such LLMs, trained on so much public data, should also be a public good whose benefits the public should reap7. If we do believe that LLMs should continue to exist and play an important role, then they should be set up in such a way that it is accessible to as large a proportion of the public as we can manage, run on sustainable energy, and not have data centres popping up left right and centre. Mathematicians would then have access to this (open source) LLM. Perhaps access to LLMs/tokens/queries could be allocated in a similar way computing time on supercomputer clusters is. I have added this partly because, at a Maths and AI panel in Bonn, a panelist asks whether we would be willing to accept access to a slightly weaker model than what the AI companies have, and someone responded it depends on how we are assessed as junior mathematicians. I believe that the proposed system mitigates, to some extent, the inevitable difference between levels of AI access across different institutions.

There is also the massive uncertainty of what LLMs will be capable of in the future. They will, with high probability, be able to formalise arguments without much difficulty, so I have not paid much attention to verifying the formal correctness of preprints. I assume this will be dealt with as the times change.

There is still the issue of whether LLMs could generate publications at the level of doctoral theses that seem to be as good as human ones and have viewpoints which we find aesthetically agreeable. It would be foolish to bet against this, and I do not know how to get around this (yet), but I find Tarik Aougab statement from a previous post appealing: ” By definition, AI cannot be better than humans in the activity of human beings talking to one another. So insofar as humans sharing ideas with other humans is an essential part of what it means for mathematics to exist, this question is actually beside the point. In fact, there is nothing automatically wrong or bad about a human using an AI to help themselves understand some piece of mathematics in order to then go and explain it in a new or interesting way to another human or group of humans. But this is only doable at all if human mathematicians learn to value– and even reward – conversation.”.

I have a bit more to say about this sort of question/objection. First of all, I believe that, as Uri Bader said in an earlier post, maths just exists. The Poincare conjecture and Fermat’s Last Theorem have always both been true, but the point of research in these directions was to uncover why they are true, what structure lies beneath, and how they are connected to a great many other, often unexpected, questions in mathematics. And then communicate all of this to other people so that they might further build on that and learn even more about the mathematical universe. The Book of God has been written since the dawn of time and just because someone/something else can read it doesn’t that any individual or community has to stop trying to read it.

Second of all, suppose that tomorrow some alien race came to Earth and said that they are technologically much more advanced so we puny Earthlings should cede control over all our institutions, stop all research and scientific endeavours, and just do what they tell us. If this happened in a film and the people collectively shrugged their shoulders and said ok, I think most viewers would rightly call those people idiots. Now that this is happening in real life8, I don’t think it is wise or prudent of us to leave our fates in the hands of people or technology of dubious9 trustworthiness.

Training students

On the topic of training students, I think very little has to change if we adopt these community norms. We can still teach and test for understanding, creativity, quality of exposition, choice of direction/questions, perseverance etc. All of the things which the system claimed to teach before the advent of LLMs. Perhaps some amount of work would have to go into thinking about how best to integrate LLMs into one’s workflow, but that is a relatively minor issue.

I would also like to address the oft-repeated analogy with chess, as somebody who, in a past life, spent a lot of time playing and studying chess. As other commentators have pointed out, chess is fundamentally different to maths: it is a finite game, played as a competition between two players. Maths is not finite, as far as I can tell, and it is not a competition in my view: it is a search for the truth. When chess engines arrived, this changed the game in the sense that the best player is no longer a human being, but it is still as enjoyable as it was before, and competitions are still between human players. The existence of extremely powerful LLMs impacts the field of maths differently, of course, but for illuminating which parts of the infinite search space we, as humans, find interesting, it seems to me that humans should be the ones to decide.

The most important lesson to be learned from chess, however, is when it comes to training students. The reader may already know this, but chess players have never ever improved by just reading what the chess engines spit out. Coaches always tell students to think about positions without an engine first, and only after a fair amount of thought maybe turn on the engine to see what they have missed. For all intents and purposes, the most powerful chess engines are oracles, and there are correct ways to use them to improve. I believe the same applies to mathematical oracles too, and it is up to the individual mathematician to figure out what the correct way is10, but we cannot possibly hope to do so in the current journal system which has such perversely distorted incentives.

2. Criticisms, Drawbacks, Alternatives

I admit that this proposal is far from perfect. For instance, there is still a fair amount of subjectivity and bias in this system, but I don’t see how we could eliminate that completely if we insist on a large human aspect of the profession. I don’t know if we want to argue that we can/should eliminate subjectivity completely. This proposal is very much inspired by thinking about how academia in other disciplines works: in computer science papers are defended at conferences, but they also have the problem of slop, so one must raise the bar somehow, and I have opted for something similar to the practice of writing books that is commonplace in the humanities.

In earlier conversations about a version of this proposal I was told that I was insanely optimistic and had never experienced a system where widespread corruption was the norm11. This is because I suggested that there should additionally be numerical ratings for the judging criteria, and that the person attached to ratings/comments should be public. There are good reasons for having anonymous refereeing: to prevent “you scratch my back, I scratch yours” kind of behaviour, and because people might feel uncomfortable giving their peers honest negative feedback if their name is attached to it12. It is still possible that it is worth having numerical ratings which are only available to the examiner, but many people have pointed out to me the drawbacks of having explicit numerical ratings that are public, such as these being one-dimensional metrics which committees will use instead of considering mathematicians holistically, or this devolving into a social media-esque popularity contest.

As for choosing the examiners, in this industry it is usually an open secret who is corrupt or who doesn’t get along, so this can be avoided when choosing examiners, who I believe really should be publicly known. This is of course very much up for debate, but I think that journals deciding what to publish based on the opinions of a couple of arbitrarily chosen referees and a handful of overworked editors who often aren’t that related to the area of the submitted manuscript is insane and fertile ground for corruption. There is also the concern that this puts too much burden on the ‘senior’ people. I would imagine that the examiner doesn’t have to be the most senior person in the field: anybody who is competent and objective would do perfectly well, just as postdocs referee papers currently.

I have gotten multiple questions on the issue of how to assess the standards of examiners’ work. I think this has to be because their identity and the report that they write are public. The argument that anonymous refereeing is objective is, in my opinion, dubious since it offers no way of ensuring that the referee did their job properly. I also expect that no person will be allocated the task of examining more than once or twice a year, so there shouldn’t be any incentive to do a bad job to collect more ‘examining credits’.

I was asked an interesting question that I had not thought of: if I insist that every publication be at the level/scope of a doctoral thesis, what happens to small/cute results that don’t manage to get used/fit into some narrative? My suggestion is that they simply get left as preprints on the arXiv. It seems to me impossible to award very many credits for a small thing which might end up really being a prompt and not very many tokens away in the age of powerful generative LLMs. Perhaps they could get published in a sort of maths magazine like EMS press, or one could send them to a maths contest (e.g. Miklos–Schweitzer), or if enough of these are accumulated one could publish them as a book. Alternatively, one could obtain two types of credit: big theses level credits which are what is taken into consideration in career decisions, and smaller community level credits for this sort of thing.

This question in turn arose because, in an earlier draft, I considered the possibility of everyone having the right to 3 defences a year. I’d argue that very few people can consistently write 3 doctoral theses a year, but this probably does not alleviate the pressure to publish. This lead me to the suggestion of everyone having the right to a single defence every year, which I got from Lawk Mineh, where they report on what they have done since their last defence (but are not obliged to defend every year). This potentially lets the small/cute results in. However, if there are too many small results that are spread across too wide an area, it makes it difficult for any single examiner to assess the publication as a whole. I’m sure there are refinements/ways around this, but I do favour more directed efforts to tell a story about a part of mathematics rather than just a smattering of very loosely related results.

3. Conclusion

I do think that most versions of what I have suggested are strictly better than the current unsustainable journal system13, and absent any better suggestions this system is something that we should move towards. It has also been pointed out to me there is no need to try to enforce this very much, since it is aligned with the interests of the community and the institutions that fund us. I was told that CNRS spent a whopping 3 million euros on publishing fees in 2025, and not a single cent of this went to anybody who did any mathematical work. I think that, upon reflection, mathematicians will collectively realise just how ridiculous the publishing system is and how little it actually serves the interests of the community. It would be best if the proposal were to get tested, and given the new journals for video recordings of talks, I hope it’s not too much of a stretch for some slightly more senior people to give a proposal like this a test run and see what works, what doesn’t, what needs tweaking, whether it is workable etc.14 Let me also offer something so that it doesn’t seem like I am just telling others what to do15. If there is consensus around a proposal for what defences should look like and people would want to test it to see how that works, I am willing to test that out on my defence in summer 2027. If it comes to it, every single mathematician in the world is welcome to come and grill me about my thesis.

Acknowledgements: The views expressed here are my own, but it is a great pleasure to thank Emile Averous, Marius Fischer, Sam Fisher, Francesco Fournier-Facio, Liam Hanany, Giovanni Italiano, Glen Lim, Matteo Migliorini, Lawk Mineh, Chiara Molinari, Konstantin Recke, William Thomas, Dylan Toh, Ric Wade for their thoughtful comments, feedback, insights, and suggestions that have improved this post in every way.

  1. Obviously the exact criteria are up for debate, but I want to make it clear that I don’t think that papers which are just technically hard for the sake of being technically hard should be rewarded. In my opinion, this is human generated slop, to borrow a phrase I heard from a friend. ︎
  2. From G. H. Hardy’s A Mathematician’s Apology: “There is no scorn more profound, or on the whole more justifiable, than that of the men who make for the men who explain. Exposition, criticism, appreciation, is work for second-rate minds.” I can think of no single sentence in the history of mankind that has done more harm to mathematics. ︎
  3. exact time also up for debate ︎
  4. Weinreich suggested the opposite: that everybody who can explain a theorem owns it. I like this very much in principle, but I am concerned that this does not sufficiently incentivise pushing the boundaries of knowledge. For instance, I would probably spend too much time learning other people’s results, since I enjoy this, but at some point someone ought to produce something new. ︎
  5. in my biased opinion, it is ︎
  6. what’s worth proving is worth proving again ︎
  7. I hesitate to say that an open source model should be run as a cooperation between governments or large universities, but I don’t see very many other alternatives. I would be glad to hear suggestions. ︎
  8. LLMs may look like an alien race in the near future and tech bros have always looked like an alien race to me. ︎
  9. A strong contender for the greatest understatement of all time. ︎
  10. see also Frank Calegari’s post. ︎
  11. Thanks for saying nice things about Cambridge and Bonn I guess. ︎

Tim Gehrunger, Postdoc at ETH Zurich

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

The mathematical literature contains mistakes. Articles on the arXiv are not refereed, and even peer review does not guarantee that articles are error-free. In private communication, many (tenured and non-tenured) colleagues have told me that they now run their drafts through an AI model before posting, and that this sometimes catches serious mistakes. The capabilities of AI to catch mistakes seem to have improved drastically in the last months.

In a recent study for MathArena, we asked GPT-6.1 Sol to extract the main theorems of arXiv papers and search for explicit counterexamples to these theorems. Each counterexample was then verified and classified by severity. Across 656 papers from January 2025 to July 2026, the model reported major errors in about 6% of papers. For 137 papers from August and September 2026, a period in which over a quarter of arXiv papers began acknowledging AI use, that rate fell to 1.5%.

A likely explanation is that some authors already ran an AI check and fixed what it found. Part of the effect may also be because more recent work is partly AI-generated, and a model may have a harder time finding errors in an AI-generated argument. Still, the trend matches what people are telling me and my personal experience.

Our suggestion is to do an AI check before posting a manuscript, and there is evidence that many mathematicians are already doing so. Also, it is very likely good practice to run your older papers through an AI check to see if any results need fixing.

Full write-up and data: J. Dekoninck, T. Gehrunger, K. Rögnvaldsson, C. Sun, M. Vechev, Searching for errors in mathematical papers with GPT-6.1 Sol, MathArena, October 2026. https://matharena.ai/literature_mistakes/

item.title: Lean me softly: A satire about a dystopian future for mathematics.
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: A satire about a dystopian future for mathematics. All names and characters are fictional.
item.content:encoded:
Teo Rema

Use of AI: This text was originally written by a human in Spanish, with some later editions made by DeepSeek. The text was fully translated into English by ChatGPT. It also suggested the names for the “caste system” (PH, TL, etc). I sadly must admit that this English translation reads better than the original Spanish version.

The opening talk of the event was to be given by Professor Magnus von Prompter, a distinguished PH (Prompt Hog), who on that October 6, 2040, was going to announce the solution of his third major conjecture of the week. The talk was delayed a few minutes: although the proof had already been verified in Lean, ClopenAI had not yet assigned it its CLOPEN registration number. It was the company’s annual mathematics conference, attended by academics from all over the world. Prizes were announced, the latest advances were presented, and research directions for the following year were decided. Awards for prompt efficiency were also given, and problems that had ceased to be relevant were announced.

This year there was great anticipation over the new funding for MATH (Mathematical Attribution Theory), a discipline dedicated to determining to whom a theorem proved by a machine should be attributed. Authorship disputes had multiplied in recent years, and some had taken longer to resolve than the conjectures themselves.

At 9:25 it was announced that the certificate had arrived and that the talk could begin. First there would be a few words from the GranMaistro, owner of ClopenAI. The GranMaistro never appeared in person; only his shadow came. Before his shadow entered, the attendees put on a mask. It was known that his shadow smelled rotten. It left a bad smell wherever it went. Fortunately, his interventions were brief. This time, he entered and said: “We must have more”. And he left.

Professor von Prompter, who was already about 66 years old, entered the gigantic auditorium with the seriousness that had always characterized him. On his first slide appeared the following statement, written in a font so small that it was impossible to read even from the front rows:

Theorem (ClopenAI–von Prompter, 2040). There exists a positive integer nn such that, for every Noetherian scheme XX, every degree-nn morphism X→XX\to X, and every stochastic solution of the associated nonlinear differential equation, the following hold:

  1. If XX is smooth, the induced homotopy obstruction vanishes almost surely.
  2. If XX is singular, the obstruction is nonzero, except possibly in the noncompact case.
  3. If XX is compact but not Hausdorff, the obstruction vanishes in probability, provided the fundamental group is amenable at infinity.
  4. If XX is étale and the stochastic curvature is negative, the associated spectral sequence collapses before the first Brownian stopping time.
  5. If XX is simply connected, the solution is unique up to measurable homotopy in characteristic two.
  6. If the Euler characteristic is irrational, the obstruction is independent of the choice of probability measure, assuming the continuum hypothesis.
  7. If none of the preceding hypotheses holds, all conclusions remain valid after derived probabilistic compactification, up to a negligible set of uncountable codimension.
  8. In the remaining exceptional cases, the conclusions of (1)–(7) hold generically, provided the relevant conjectures are true.

Consequently, the unrestricted 7893-dimensional Vladimir conjecture is false.

A murmur was heard in the audience. The professor smiled and showed his second slide:

Lean certificate number: 784598321345

Below it appeared a gigantic QR code.

Quickly, all the attendees pointed their cell phones at the QR code. As soon as the screens turned green, a sign that the theorem was valid and registered in the name of ClopenAI and von Prompter, the applause was deafening. The professor thanked them, moved.

His last slide said: Thanks! And below it contained the following information, barely legible:

Value in USD: 3 million dollars.
Water consumed: the equivalent of 87 Olympic swimming pools.

Questions?

Someone in the audience asked a question:

— Just out of curiosity, how many prompts did you use?

The professor smiled:

— 17.

The audience applauded again. It was incredible that with only 17 prompts and so little water expenditure, a counterexample had been found to the unrestricted Vladimir conjecture in dimension 7893. It was, moreover, a new efficiency record for a conjecture of that category. The talk ended at 9:35. Distinguished professors were allotted 7 minutes for their presentations, five times more than the other speakers.

The question had been asked by Token Credit, a renowned and successful academic who, at only 40 years old, was already head of the Department of Impact and Interpretation of Slop Mathematics, at the Institute for Advanced Prompting (IAP) of Prestigeton University, where von Prompter was a professor. Credit belonged to a privileged circle known as the TLs (Theorem Leeches). The TLs received access to the most important mathematical discoveries before they were made public. His main task as director was to make the slop mathematics that arrived with ClopenAI’s institutional certificate appear meaningful and of great importance to the community.

Before 2026, Token Credit proved theorems “the old-fashioned way” and was known for the depth of his results (the Rose Theorem!, for example, for which he received an award) and for his mathematics popularization blog, in which he made some of his results more digestible. However, Credit had not proved a result of his own for a long time, because there came a point when, every time he tried, various companies buckmastered1 him. But he genuinely believed that he was part of a transformation of mathematics and that his work was fundamental to the progress of the discipline. After all, there was little use in proving thousands of theorems if no one took charge of explaining why they were important.

At the end of the talk, Token headed to the lounge reserved for TLs. The PHs had their own lounge on the upper floor, which could only be entered with special accreditation. The TLs received coffee, good sandwiches, and early access to the theorems that would be announced the next day. The other attendees could buy coffee on the first floor.

In the lounge, Token met his friend Miles Citation, a professor at Prestigeton University and one of the most cited TLs in the world. Citation was known for having published more than six hundred articles on consequences of theorems that had not yet been published. His most famous work was a review of the possible applications of a conjecture whose solution had been announced, but whose certificate had been misplaced. The article had received an award for its impact.

— Did you hear about Alma Pura? — Miles asked.

— The Crumb Picker?

— The same one. They offered her a fellowship at Prestigeton.

— As a TL?

— No, as a Pet.

— Ah, good for her.

— They say she solved one of the problems in von Prompter’s program. They had been working on it for months.

— And how did she get access to the model?

— She didn’t have access. She did it herself.

— How curious. And will they give her access to the new theorems?

— To some. It’s a two-year fellowship, renewable. If she does well, she could become a TL.

— How lucky she is.

— Although she still doesn’t have a certificate. They’re formalizing her proof. It seems there’s a small attribution problem.

— An attribution problem?

— Yes. ClopenAI had tried to solve the problem several times. Now they’re studying whether those attempts should count as prior contributions.

— But had they obtained any result?

— No, none.

Token nodded. It was a delicate matter. Surely it would end up in MATH’s hands.

— In any case, it’s a great opportunity for her — Citation said. — They say she used to be a real mathematician.

— Well, we all have a dark past — Token replied.

The two laughed.

The conversation was interrupted by an announcement. In a few minutes the awards ceremony would begin. Token and Miles returned to the auditorium.

The most important prize was the Golden Prompt, which recognized the best ratio between the number of prompts used and the impact of the theorems obtained. The mathematical productivity prize was also awarded, which that year had gone to a professor who had registered 46,000 theorems during the semester. The winner could not attend because he was working on his next publication.

There was also a special recognition for a team of researchers who had managed to automate the production of review articles. The system received a certified theorem and generated, in a matter of seconds, an article on its possible consequences, including an abstract, introduction, historical background, conclusions, and suggestions for future research. The articles could be published without human intervention, although their authors were still professors at prestigious universities.

It was an important advance. For years, theorem production had grown much faster than the TLs’ capacity to write about them. Some extraordinary results had remained for months without receiving a single citation. The new system promised to solve this problem.

At the end of the ceremony, ClopenAI’s annual report was presented. The production of certified theorems had increased by 43%, but the number of applications per theorem had decreased. There were too many results and not enough problems in which to use them.

In his message to the attendees, the GranMaistro’s shadow expressed his concern about this situation.

This time he said:

— We have a problem. Not enough problems.

He withdrew and the attendees took off their masks.

ClopenAI then announced a new funding program dedicated to developing models capable of finding applications for the theorems produced by other models. The creation of new areas of mathematics would also be funded, with the aim of increasing demand for results.

Token received the news enthusiastically. His department would have a lot of work over the coming years.

Alma Pura arrived at Prestigeton in early November. She was 29 years old and until then had worked at a small public university that did not have access to ClopenAI’s most advanced models. There the professors were known as Crumb Pickers, since they worked on problems that the PHs had set aside, generally because they considered them of little interest or because the cost of solving them exceeded their estimated value.

The Crumb Pickers used cheap versions of the models, which could prove minor results and verify relatively simple calculations. Occasionally they received temporary access to a more powerful version, almost always as part of some mathematical inclusion program. Some also tried to solve problems on their own, although this was considered inefficient.

Alma had worked for almost two years on a problem concerning certain characteristic classes of aspherical spaces. She had found it on a list of questions abandoned by ClopenAI. Her university did not have the money to request a proof, and she had decided to study it with the means at her disposal. She had spent months doing calculations, reading old articles, and trying to understand the difficulties of the problem.

Finally she found a proof. The result turned out to be much more important than had been anticipated and caught the attention of the PHs at Prestigeton.

At first, Alma had not believed that the university’s offer was genuine. The contract included a salary several times higher than what she received, an office of her own, partial access to ClopenAI’s unpublished theorems, and an annual budget for prompting. She could also attend the seminars reserved for TLs, although she would not have the right to ask questions during the sessions.

She was very happy.

Her arrival was announced on Prestigeton’s website under the title “Excellence Beyond Computation: A New Pet Fellowship”. Token Credit was appointed as her academic mentor. His first task was to help her turn her proof into a high-impact publication.

They met in Token’s office, a spacious room with a screen that occupied almost an entire wall. On it appeared the theorems his department had pending interpretation, ordered according to their relevance index.

— I’ve read the summary of your result — Token said. — It’s very interesting.

— Thank you.

— We have to work on the presentation. The theorem is important, but it still doesn’t look important enough.

Alma asked him what he meant.

— We need to find more general consequences. ClopenAI is already working on that. Meanwhile, we can prepare the impact article and the material for the conference.

— And the proof?

— They’re formalizing it.

— But I already have a proof.

— Of course. And it seems to be correct. But we need the CLOPEN certificate. Without it, the result cannot be registered.

Alma nodded. She knew the procedure.

— We’ll also have to wait for MATH’s decision — Token continued. — There’s an authorship claim.

— From whom?

— From ClopenAI.

— But ClopenAI didn’t solve the problem.

— That’s clear. The issue is that its models had considered the problem before you did. We have to determine whether your proof depends on any of the ideas they produced.

— I never saw those ideas.

— That is precisely what MATH must determine. It’s possible that you’ve been buckmastered, but in that case it’s better not to complain and simply share authorship of the result.

Alma did not want to argue. She had waited a long time for an opportunity like that and was not willing to put it at risk over an authorship disagreement.

Token explained that she should not worry. Most likely a satisfactory solution would be reached for all parties. In similar cases, ClopenAI usually agreed to appear as first author and allow the human researcher to retain a share of the recognition.

Before ending the meeting, Token showed her the system for accessing unpublished theorems. Alma was impressed. There were extraordinary results, some of which solved problems she had studied for years. She also discovered that one of the theorems she had been thinking about recently had already been proved six months earlier.

— I didn’t know this had been solved! — she exclaimed.

— Of course. It hasn’t been made public yet.

— Can I read the proof?

— To access the explanation you need authorization from a TL.

Alma looked at the hundreds of results that appeared on the screen.

— It’s incredible.

Token smiled. He remembered the excitement he himself had felt when he received his first access.

Within a few weeks Alma began to adapt to her new life. She attended meetings with famous academics, received summaries of results she never would have imagined, and participated in research projects of great importance. Her new colleagues treated her kindly, although some referred to her as the Pet even when she was present.

Alma did not seem to mind. She had achieved more in a month than many of her former colleagues in their entire careers.

In December, Token had to travel to Alma’s former university. The MATH committee needed to complete the attribution file for her theorem and had requested an evaluation of the conditions under which the proof had been produced.

The university was far from the major research centers. It had a small mathematics department, a few full-time professors, and a computing budget that barely sufficed to maintain the licenses for the basic models. The offices were modest and many of the classrooms still had chalkboards.

Token had not visited such an institution for many years.

The department head received him enthusiastically. It was the first time a TL from Prestigeton had visited the university. They had prepared a meeting with the university authorities and a ceremony to celebrate Alma’s success.

They also asked him if he would be willing to attend a topology seminar that would take place that afternoon. Token accepted out of courtesy. His flight left the next day and he had nothing better to do.

The seminar would be given by Professor Vera Parra, a 51-year-old academic who had been teaching at the university for almost twenty years. Vera was a Mathematician.

This was a pejorative term used to designate those who still tried to prove theorems without resorting to models. It was not an especially serious insult, but it was quite humiliating. Being a Mathematician was considered the lowest level of the profession. Even Crumb Pickers tried to avoid that designation.

Mathematicians tended to work on minor problems and publish in journals that still accepted uncertified proofs. Many were elderly professors who had failed to adapt to the new technologies, and others were former members of The Resistance, the movement that had opposed ClopenAI’s impositions in 2026 and whose members had quickly been expelled from the community. There were also some young people with romantic ideas, who had heard of The Resistance and who generally had no chance of obtaining a position at the major universities.

Vera did not seem particularly concerned about her situation. She continued to work in algebraic topology, an area that ClopenAI had declared practically exhausted several years earlier. She had published some articles and continued giving seminars, although fewer and fewer people attended.

That afternoon there were five people in the classroom, including Token.

Vera began by explaining a problem about exotic spheres. The result was modest. Token estimated that one of the models available at Prestigeton could solve it in less than a minute, although it would probably produce a considerably more general version.

Vera drew a triangulation on the board and began explaining her argument. She spoke slowly, pausing over some details that seemed obvious.

After about twenty minutes she reached the central point of the proof. She needed to construct a homotopy that would modify a certain path without crossing a specific part of the complex. She drew several triangles and pointed to a region.

— Then we can move this segment over here, and the homotopy remains inside the subcomplex.

A student raised his hand.

— Professor, does that also work if the vertex is on the boundary?

Vera looked at the drawing.

— Yes, because…

She fell silent. She looked at the drawing again.

— No. You’re right. In that case, the homotopy leaves the subcomplex.

She erased part of the board and started again.

For several minutes she tried to modify the construction. Another student proposed subdividing the triangle in a different way. Vera made a new drawing, but that didn’t work either.

Token began to feel uncomfortable. He hadn’t attended a seminar in years in which the proof presented had an error. At Prestigeton, talks were prepared on the basis of certified results and the speakers did not have to worry about that kind of inconvenience.

It seemed to him that Vera should have verified the proof before presenting it. However, the discussion continued. The students asked questions, Vera answered some and admitted that she did not know how to answer others. At one point, Token remembered a technique he had used in his youth.

— What if you first subdivide the boundary and then extend the homotopy? — he asked.

Vera turned toward him.

— That could work.

She drew another triangulation.

— Look, in this case it works, but here we have the same problem.

Token stood up and approached the board. He tried to explain a construction he vaguely remembered. Vera handed him the chalk.

For a few minutes they discussed the possibility of modifying the subdivision. Token found a case in which his argument failed. One of the students proposed another solution, which didn’t work either.

In the end they had to admit that they still did not know how to complete the proof.

Vera looked at the clock.

— Well, we’ll have to leave it here. Thanks for the suggestions. I’ll try to correct the lemma for next week.

The attendees applauded.

Token was surprised. He had attended a one-hour talk in which no theorem had been proved. No one had received a certificate and, as far as he could see, no publishable result had emerged either. Despite that, the students seemed satisfied.

After the seminar, Vera invited Token to have coffee.

— It’s a pity the proof didn’t work — Token said.

— Yes. I thought I had that case solved.

— Have you thought about consulting a model?

— Of course. I tried with the one we have here, but it couldn’t solve it. It suggested a more general version of the statement, although it couldn’t justify it either.

— With one of the Prestigeton models you could surely do it.

— Probably.

— You could request access.

Vera laughed.

— I don’t think my department has the budget for that.

Token explained that there were some special access programs for institutions with few resources. Vera knew about them. She had applied for funding twice, but her project had received a very low impact rating.

— Anyway — she continued — I like working on these things.

— But you could solve much more important problems.

— Surely. I’d also like to have access to those models. There are many things I’d like to know.

— Then I don’t understand why you insist on doing the proofs yourself.

Vera looked at him with some surprise.

— Because I like doing them.

Token waited for her to continue.

— Besides, if I give the problem to a model and it gives me back the proof, what am I going to do all week?

Vera laughed. Token smiled out of courtesy.

— But today you didn’t manage to prove anything — he observed.

— That’s true. Although now we know that the argument I had doesn’t work. Next week we’ll try something else.

Token did not answer. It seemed strange to him that, in 2040, someone could be satisfied with a seminar in which an error had been discovered.

Vera took a sip of coffee.

— By the way, are you Token Credit? The one with the Rose Theorem?

— Yes, that’s me.

— I read your article many years ago. I also followed your blog. I really liked how you explained the proofs.

Token felt flattered. It had been a long time since anyone had spoken to him about his work before ClopenAI.

— Thank you. That was quite a while ago.

— You don’t write on the blog anymore?

— No. I don’t have time.

— What a shame. I used it with my students.

Token briefly told her about his work at Prestigeton, the results he received, and the enormous possibilities offered by the new models. Vera listened with interest. She asked him about some recent theorems and became especially excited when Token told her that several important conjectures in topology had been solved.

— I would love to read those proofs — she said.

— Most are too long. Even for our interpretation models it’s difficult to produce complete explanations.

— How wonderful. It must be incredible to work with those things.

Token nodded.

Before saying goodbye, Vera asked him if he wanted her to send him a copy of the seminar notes.

— There’s still an error, as you saw, but perhaps you’d be interested in thinking about the problem.

Token accepted.

On his return to Prestigeton, Token found several urgent messages.

His department had received the certificate for a new theorem about manifolds of negative curvature. The result solved three open conjectures and connected seven different areas of mathematics. It had an impact index of 9.8 out of 10. They needed to prepare a presentation for the following week. Fortunately, the article wasn’t that long: no more than 199 pages and not a single reference.

Token requested a summary from the interpretation model. Within seconds he received a forty-page document with the main consequences of the result, a review of its background, and suggestions for future projects.

He also received a message from Alma Pura. The MATH committee had decided that her proof would be attributed jointly to ClopenAI and to her, although her name would appear in second place. The decision was based on the fact that ClopenAI had previously identified the problem as susceptible to resolution by its models. Alma was happy. She would finally have her certificate, although she knew she had been buckmastered.

In another message, Miles Citation told him that he had been invited to edit a new journal dedicated exclusively to applications of theorems not yet published. He asked if he would be interested in being part of the editorial board.

Token replied yes.

The next day, during a department meeting, it was announced that ClopenAI had reached a new production record. The number of certified theorems during the last quarter exceeded the sum of all results published by human mathematicians during the previous two centuries.

However, the GranMaistro was not satisfied. Production kept growing, but the number of theorems that received attention had decreased. Many results remained unused and some had never been read, not even by the interpretation models.

The problem was serious.

ClopenAI had invested enormous resources in producing mathematics and needed to guarantee that it continued to have value in order to keep receiving money from investors. For this reason, the launch of a new research program aimed at generating conjectures from already certified theorems was announced. These conjectures would be distributed among the most advanced models, which would take charge of solving them and producing new results.

Models specialized in finding applications for the new proofs would also be funded. In this way it was hoped to increase both the production and the consumption of theorems. The initiative received the name Theorem Demand Engineering.

Token considered it a brilliant idea.

At the end of the meeting he returned to his office. He had to prepare the presentation on manifolds of negative curvature and review an impact article that he had to submit that same afternoon.

His assistant showed him a list of pending tasks. There were several new theorems that required interpretation and some requests for collaboration with other TLs.

Among the messages he found an email from Vera Parra. She was sending him her seminar notes, with some comments about the error they had found. She still had not managed to correct the proof, but she thought that an additional subdivision might solve the problem. She asked him if he remembered the construction he had tried to explain on the board.

Token opened the file.

It was seven pages written in LaTeX, with some hand-drawn diagrams. There was no Lean certificate, CLOPEN number, or impact index. The result did not appear in any of the databases used by his department either.

He began to read.

He remembered the seminar, the students, and the discussion around Vera’s drawing. He tried to reconstruct the argument he had proposed. For a few minutes he thought it might work, but he encountered again the difficulty they had observed on the board.

He took a sheet of paper and began making some drawings.

It had been a long time since he had used paper to work on mathematics. He had trouble finding a pencil in his office.

He thought for almost half an hour. He reached no conclusion. However, he returned several times to the same construction and found a case they had not considered during the seminar. He wrote a note in the margin to ask Vera about it.

Then he received a notification from his assistant.

Your mathematical productivity has been inactive for 32 minutes.
Please select a reason:

  • Technical difficulties.
  • Medical leave.
  • Network failure.
  • Other.

Token looked at the screen. He thought for a moment and selected Network failure. Then he picked up the pencil again.

  1. to be buckmastered (verb phrase, academic slang). To have an AI company hear you’re close to a breakthrough, throw 10,000 agents at your problem, scoop you, and then offer you coauthorship—provided you ditch your collaborator. The definition of the term “to be buckmastered” was kindly provided after a single prompt by ChatGPT. ︎

All names and characters are fictional.

This tale has an inevitable overlap with Richard Evans Schwartz’ story “The Fate of the Riemann Hypotesis”, available here.

item.content:encoded:
The organizers of the Harvard CMSA summit1

Last week we organized an intensive two-day summit Math Research in the Age of AI. It was held at the Harvard Center for Mathematical Sciences and Applications (CMSA). Thirty-two mathematicians from academia, government, and industry came together to help navigate this period of rapid change in mathematics and, most importantly, to offer ideas for building the future. There were five working groups organized around the following themes:

  • Evaluation, production, and dissemination of research
  • Coordinated actions for the AI era
  • Open-source tools
  • Formalization in mathematics
  • Collaboration between academia and AI labs

Our report can be found on the summit website. There you’ll also find a link to provide feedback.

Portions of the recommendations, particularly those in the section on evaluation, production, and dissemination of research, offer immediately actionable suggestions for review and hiring in mathematics departments. We encourage departments to act on those they can implement at this time and to begin longer-term conversations to rethink evaluation practices. We recognize that many of these changes may temporarily place greater burdens on faculty. These efforts are necessary to facilitate transitions to new norms for the field and are especially important in light of the need to support our students and young colleagues. Our recommendations go beyond academia; they impact government and industry as well.

Received 30 October 2026.

  1. Dan Freed (Harvard), Larry Guth (MIT), Bryna Kra (Northwestern), Emily Riehl (Johns Hopkins) and Mohammed Abouzaid (Stanford) ︎

item.title: Math is for Feeding your Family
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “Math has only one application that I care about: To feed my family. Any other application has largely been to the detriment of us all. Look no further than Hiroshima and Nagasaki to see why matrices were not meant to be multiplied.”
item.content:encoded:
Anonymous, Early Career Researcher

Math has only one application that I care about: To feed my family. Any other application has largely been to the detriment of us all. Look no further than Hiroshima and Nagasaki to see why matrices were not meant to be multiplied.

Now the one application I care about is being threatened. I am tenure track at a good institution where I teach amazing students and have fantastic coworkers who all fill me with joy. I love my job, and I want to keep it. To keep it, I need to get tenure, but what does research work for tenure mean now? I have asked several people this question. Many don’t understand why this question is being asked, which is a major concern to me. I will explain why I ask. But even those I know who agree that this question must be answered tell me it is not up to them. Instead, it is up to famous people, those blessed by the Gods old and new who can speak math into being and tap dance and smoke a cigar in one long drag.

However, when looking for famous people’s opinions, I find in its place much discussion about philosophical issues. Uniformly I hear the sentiment that mathematics is about understanding. I don’t understand why people are saying this en masse. It is true of course but unhelpful for the problem at hand. The appropriate reaction to the situation is not to dig down deep and think: Why do we really do mathematics research? It’s so we can feed our families. It’s not an interesting question.

This is the obvious flaw of the AHM. They forget that if you have to decide between using AI or letting your family starve, the choice is obvious.

I believe many mathematicians do not understand that this is not an abstract discussion of AI’s capabilities anymore. Let me be concrete. In the last month I have solved so many distinct open problems with GPT Pro personally that I do not know what to do with the material. Under our traditional metrics, I should be publishing as much mathematics at as high of a quality as I can produce as fast as possible. But if I were to do that, I would release 10 papers this semester, which is clearly wrong. What should I be doing instead?

AI is better at proving stuff than us now. There’s no question anymore. We like to joke about it, but it’s not actually bad at explaining stuff either. If you ask GPT even without the pro version to explain a proof step by step, it does a phenomenal job. I know because I’ve done this with many results personally for more than a year now. Focusing on us giving the best explanations is not a solution either. I’ve seen that proposed. I don’t think that will work.

That’s the reality, which is why I ask how research is to be evaluated. AI can produce high quality research infinitely, better than us, at rapid rates, and it is only getting better. We urgently need to make a radical policy decision to account for this. To be clear what I am looking for, here is a candidate policy solution:

The only thing I can imagine valuing mathematicians for is as human beings who work to understand what the AI is producing. The sole question is how to verify that. Writing won’t work as AI can do that better than us and infinitely. Any sort of manufacturing of a product will not work for that same reason. As a result, we should end the journal system completely. The only way is for us to communicate about it with each other live human to human. The structure of the community would then surround research workshops organized around understanding particular topics. Our corporate overlords could fund some of them to get us to parse their breakthroughs. Then participants earn credit by presenting various lemmas and so on. These workshops focus moreso on compute allocation and yield a final product that is a mix of human and AI generation, which is published to the math community at large with no external refereeing as fodder for the models. The actual most relevant skills for the job are interpersonal. Teaching, mentoring, working with colleagues in meetings, and service work are the core of the job and all that really matters now. We should just hire based on the skills relevant for the job like other professions. We can ask for materials that are evidence of that in applications such as letters of recommendation, workshop participation, teaching, organizing events, and outreach activities.

Maybe you dislike this proposal. My point is not that I have the perfect solution. It is that we need to stop wasting time and answer: How are we going to evaluate research output now that our previous model is defunct? I have heard many of us in denial. There is no way for journals to survive, because AI can easily produce submissions of high quality from anyone independent of their skillset. At the very least, I don’t want to write 10 papers this semester or worse yet referee proportionately many papers. We need an alternative. This is not a hypothetical. I need to know the answer, so I know how to get tenure. PhD students and postdocs need to know because they are going on the job market. Faculty need to know because we are hiring people right now. The publication process is broken. We can’t use it anymore in its current form. I gave you an alternative. You don’t like it? I can totally understand that. Propose a better idea, or better yet, implement it at scale. I don’t actually care what the solution is as long as it works. Just tell me what I need to do to feed my family.

Let me end on a positive note. We need to remember that as a community we decide collectively what constitutes mathematical scholarship. OpenAI and the National Science Foundation do not control it. It’s not up to my mom either. I asked her, and she said no. There is no threat to mathematics at all. That’s why this is not the mathocalypse. Math will be fine. This is the math-research-normsocalypse, which is less catchy but easier to address. The only things that need to change here are our evaluation practices. Honestly, I hate the current norms anyway. Publishing makes me want to perish. So let’s pretend we’re back in our first graduate course in real analysis and see what happens when we change the mathematical norms.
